also: put it out of your mind

evidence: Cic. Sen. 21: oblītum quō locō thēsaurum obruisset
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: the person forgotten in the genitive, a thing in the genitive or the accusative; less often an infinitive, forget to (Petr. 49.1), or a question, forget where or what (Cic. Sen. 21). “Don’t forget” is nōlī oblīvīscī (Traupman 163), or mementō with an infinitive (see remember).

terms.gloss: slip from the memory: excidit mihi, it has slipped my mind
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, intransitive: what is forgotten is the subject, the person in the dative
evidence: Cic. Att. 6.1.7: mihi nōn excidisse illud
Traupman 107: it has slipped my mind, memoriā excidit
terms.comment: Literally “fall out”: also ex animō or dē memoriā excidere (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: unlearn, forget what one has learned
evidence: Plaut. Am. 688: quī quod didicit id dēdiscit

terms.gloss: it slipped my mind (to do), I forgot (to)
terms.grammar: impersonal: the thing forgotten is the subject or an infinitive, the person in the accusative
evidence: Cic. Att. 7.18.3: dē Dionȳsiō, fugit mē ad tē anteā scrībere (Lewis & Short s.v. fugiō)
Traupman 104: it slipped my mind to write to you, fūgit mē ad tē scrībere
terms.comment: Literally “it escaped me”. Traupman prints the perfect, fūgit; Cicero’s present fugit mē serves for what one has just realised one forgot. With a clause, tē nōn fugit is “you are well aware”.

phrases.latin: sē oblītum esse exinterāre. — quid, oblītus?
phrases.english: he said he had forgotten to gut it. — What, forgotten?

phrases.latin: nec vērō quemquam senem audīvī oblītum quō locō thēsaurum obruisset
phrases.english: and I never heard of an old man who forgot where he had buried his treasure

phrases.latin: sed plānē tē intellegere voluī mihi nōn excidisse illud quod tū ad mē quibusdam litterīs scrīpsissēs
phrases.english: but I wanted you to see quite clearly that I had not forgotten what you once wrote to me in a letter
